title: Navi — browser-agent bridge and telemetry host
description: One dashboard for both Navi services: the MCP bridge's containment and session metrics, and the ingestion host's request, rate-limit, retention and store metrics. Every panel reads a series the services actually export on their unauthenticated /metrics endpoints; nothing here is a placeholder.

list.name: datasource
list.label: Prometheus
list.description: Select the Prometheus that scrapes both Navi /metrics endpoints. Every panel binds to this variable, so an imported dashboard needs no per-panel editing.

panels.title: Scrape targets up
panels.description: Prometheus-synthesized `up`, one series per configured Navi target. 0 means the service is not answering /metrics at all, which is also what its container healthcheck probes.

panels.title: Containment enforced
panels.description: 1 while the private-network policy is active, 0 once NAVI_ALLOW_LOCAL_NETWORK=1 disabled it. Anything other than 1 on a deployment that serves untrusted agents is a dropped control; NaviContainmentEnforcementDisabled alerts on it.

panels.title: MCP sessions (open vs ceiling)
panels.description: navi_mcp_sessions against its configured ceiling. A dashboard that only showed the open count could not tell quiet from saturated. Every session is a real Chromium, so size the ceiling against the container's memory limit.

panels.title: Refusals per second by category
panels.description: The rate view of the containment counter, split by the category the MCP service classified: metadata_endpoint, private_ipv4, loopback_or_local, cgnat_or_multicast, ipv6_special or dns_rebinding_rejected. A steady rate is an agent probing; a single spike is usually a fixture the deployment forgot to allow.

panels.title: Containment violations by category (cumulative)
panels.description: navi_containment_violations is a process-lifetime counter per category, so this panel resets whenever the MCP service restarts. Read it for the shape of the audit trail; read the rate panel for what is happening now.

panels.title: Host request throughput by route and status
panels.description: Rate of navi_host_requests_total, labelled by the closed route set and the status the host answered. This is also the closest thing to a latency signal that exists: no latency histogram is exported yet, so a route whose throughput collapses while its error rate rises is the observable symptom, not a p99.

panels.title: Store bytes on disk
panels.description: navi_host_store_bytes is the size of the active store file: the SQLite database, or the append-only JSONL log when the runtime fell back to it. Watch it against the volume it lives on, and against navi_host_pruned_records_total - growth with no prunes is a retention problem, not a traffic problem.

panels.title: Retention prunes and records removed
panels.description: navi_host_prune_events_total counts every prune invocation - the six-hourly sweep and the tenant maintenance route alike - and navi_host_pruned_records_total what those prunes deleted. A flat event counter over a day means NAVI_RETENTION_DAYS is 0 or the sweep is not running.

panels.title: Rate-limited tenants
panels.description: navi_host_rate_limited_total per tenant: 429s the token bucket emitted on the two ingest routes. A sustained rate means the tenant is genuinely busier than its ceiling, or its forwarder is retrying; because a rate-limited MCP forward counts as failed rather than being retried, it is also a gap in that tenant's audit trail.

panels.title: Forwarder queue depth and losses
panels.description: The MCP bridge queues each refusal for the host and never blocks the request it describes: forwarded means accepted, failed means the host refused or never answered, dropped means the 256-event backlog was full, and queued is what is waiting now. Any movement in dropped or failed is an audit record the tenant cannot read back.

panels.title: Active tenants in the rate limiter
panels.description: navi_host_active_tenants is the current size of the token-bucket map. Buckets are forgotten after ten idle minutes, so this is who is active now, not how many tenants exist - a number that tracks the map rather than the registry is exactly what makes an unbounded-rate-limit bug visible.
